title: Does MIS-PO Need Ratio-Based Trajectory Selection? A Random-Rejection Mechanism Test

contributions.purpose: Isolates whether MIS-PO's stability gains come from its ratio-based trajectory selection criterion or merely from rejecting some trajectories.
contributions.mechanism: A three-condition controlled experiment: full MIS-PO, TokenOnly (token-level filtering only, no trajectory filtering), and RandomTraj (random trajectory rejection matched to MIS-PO's acceptance rate).
contributions.evaluation: Run on MATH-500 with staleness s* = 256, holding acceptance count fixed while randomizing selection.
contributions.source_quote: We design a three-condition experiment: MIS-PO (full method), TokenOnly (token-level filtering only), and RandomTraj (random trajectory rejection matching MIS-PO's acceptance rate).

contributions.purpose: Shows that MIS-PO's trajectory-level filtering is actively harmful and its ratio-based criterion is counterproductive.
contributions.mechanism: Compares accuracy of the three conditions under identical staleness and acceptance rates.
contributions.evaluation: TokenOnly (59.25%) outperforms MIS-PO (2.85%) by 56.4 percentage points; RandomTraj (40.85%) outperforms MIS-PO by 38.0pp at identical acceptance rates, i.e., random selection achieves 14x better accuracy than ratio-based selection.
contributions.source_quote: TokenOnly (59.25%) dramatically outperforms MIS-PO (2.85%) by 56.4 percentage points. RandomTraj (40.85%) outperforms MIS-PO by 38.0pp despite identical acceptance rates...

contributions.purpose: Explains the mechanism behind MIS-PO's failure.
contributions.mechanism: Analyzes the trajectories retained by MIS-PO's narrow bounds [0.996, 1.001], showing they are closest to the reference policy and carry minimal learning signal (sigma = 0.0012) while RandomTraj-accepted trajectories have 22x higher variance (sigma = 0.026).
contributions.evaluation: Variance analysis of accepted trajectories; token-level importance weighting alone approaches published GRPO baselines within 5pp.
contributions.source_quote: Analysis reveals that MIS-PO's narrow bounds [0.996, 1.001] systematically retain trajectories closest to the reference policy, which carry minimal learning signal. Token-level importance weighting alone suffices and approaches published GRPO baselines.

self_declared_provenance.quote: MIS-PO (Huang et al., 2026) extends this with dual-level filtering: token-level clipping combined with trajectory-level bounds on geometric mean importance ratios... Our work directly tests whether such trajectory-level filtering provides genuine benefits or merely reduces effective batch size.
Our investigation reveals that overly restrictive trajectory filtering can paradoxically harm stability by inducing gradient starvation.

notes: Negative-result / debunking paper: it is a mechanism test refuting MIS-PO's trajectory-level filtering rather than proposing a new method. No explicit 'Our contributions are' bullet list on pages 1-2; contributions derived from abstract and introduction prose.
